utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner, and Daryl Mundis, assisted today by Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel, Stephane Bourgon co-counsel, and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the appearances for the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Kubura today, Mr. Rodney Dixon assisted by Mr. Nermin Mulalic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet everyone present, the Prosecution, our expert witness, who is appearing for the last time, I hope. That depends on the Defence. I greed members of the Defence and I greet General Hadzihasanovic and Mr. Kubura. On behalf of the Chamber I would also like to greet everyone else in and around the courtroom. As I have already said as I said yesterday, we should be concluding with the testimony of the expert witness today. I have a series of questions to put to him and I will then give the floor to the Prosecution and to the Defence. So if we can then complete this witness's week of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have a few preliminary questions that concern yourself. In annex 1 of your report, you said that you were in the United States in 1997, 1998 and 1999. And I believe that you attended an American military school. Could you provide us with a little information about -- of the course that you followed in the United States.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two-thirds of the time that I spent in the USA I spent in Texas, in Los Angeles and an American school for learning American English. I spent the remainder of the time that I was there in the postgraduate naval school in Montero which is between Los Angeles and San Francisco. And I studied the subject of material resources, or rather I studied the use and planning of material resources that the state has to defend itself. When attending that course, there was a 15- to 20-day visit to Washington, Washington DC, the state bodies in that town were visited, and we visited the UN building in New York.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yesterday, in response to a question, you said that you were currently working on a doctoral thesis. What is the subject of your Ph.D. Thesis? Does it have to do with military matters or does it concern some other subject?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: My masters thesis concerned political and military preparations for an aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina and its implementation in the territory of north-eastern Bosnia. This naturally included the entire political and military status of the former Yugoslavia in the pre-war years, the break up of Yugoslavia and the course of the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina. And now, since I didn't touch on the subject of Sarajevo as the capital in that thesis, I am now trying to obtain permission to deal with the subject, or to deal with the subject of Sarajevo and its role and, naturally, I would compare this with the political and diplomatic situation that would be the subject of my Ph.D. thesis and I might thus contribute to clarifying the overall political and military situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and, in particular, in Sarajevo in the course of the war by dealing with such a subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question that concerns yourself. In annex 52 of your report, there's a reference to page 133. It's a footnote and the footnote is entitled "aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina". This page, which is in your report, has it been extracted from an article, or a book?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I'd have to have a look at that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Have a look at annex 52.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is in fact my statement and it's contained in the book that I published, in this form. This is my statement with regard to all the events from the time an attack was launched on the republic of Slovenia, because in 1990 I was serving in Ljubljana, the capital of Slovenia and I was the commander of a motorised battalion there. After that military situation had been resolved in Slovenia I then received an order from Belgrade to move with my battalion and my equipment from Ljubljana to Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the Zenica barracks. That was on the 20th of August 1991. And then, two months later, on the 20th of October, 1991, in the same way, by order from Belgrade, I was moved from Zenica together with my entire battalion, men and equipment, to the Tuzla barracks, which is in the north-eastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I was supposed to go with my battalion from there and launch an attack against the Republic of Croatia, to be more specific, against the town of Vukovar. A few days ago I mentioned this. Up to that point in time many of my subordinate officers, non-Serb officers, Macedonians, Croats, Slovenians, Muslims, Bosniaks, Albanians, had already deserted en masse, as well as a large number of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will interrupt you there. Was your book translated into English or is it only available in your own language?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment it's only available in the Bosnian language. If possible, it will be translated in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will move on to another subject. As a corps commander, could you describe a typical day for a corps commander starting by what a corps commander does in the morning, and right up until the late afternoon. What does a corps commander do? Could you split this up into two parts? Could you describe his role when the day has come and could you describe a day when there is intensive action as in defensive, authentic action, so that we can be familiar with the sort of activities that a corps commander is involved in, in the course of an average or typical day.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: You yourselves have said it would be best to break this question up into two versions. Firstly, to deal with what a corps commander does in peacetime conditions and the second version would be what the corps commander -- what a corps commander does in wartime conditions. And there would be certain sub-versions, for example, what a corps commander does in the course of offensive or defensive action. In peacetime conditions, a corps commander, just like all other officers in peacetime, goes to work, just like all the other officers and like all other citizens or workers who go to work in a factory. When he arrives at work the corps commander has to receive a report when he enters the barracks, the garrison where his command is located, where his office is located, and one of the barracks of his units. If the corps is big he has a number of barracks and a number of units and somewhere in the central part of the area where his corps is deployed he has his office. He receives a report from the duty officers as soon as he enters the barracks. The duty reports to him with the unit lined up, with the guard and military police lined up and the duty officer reports to him on the situation in the entire corps over the last 24 hours, or rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report from the duty officer, is it an oral report? Or is there a written report as well?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both a written and an oral report. The oral report is given in the morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what time is this report provided?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: This depends on when one starts working. If one starts working at 7 or 8 that's when the report is provided. The corps commander has to arrive punctually at a minute to 8.00. If works start at 8.00, he has to arrive at the gate at that time, and that is where he is welcomed by the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is the case for all the corps in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or was this a situation that was specific to the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the corps commander in peacetime conditions. Not a single corps commander had such possibilities until after the war. I'm speaking about corps commanders when the JNA existed, in peacetime conditions. Later I will talk about the conditions in the course of the war. In peacetime conditions, when the JNA existed, the commander would receive an oral report that related to the situation over the last 24 hours. This takes about ten minutes. He then briefly reviews the units or the guards and then naturally he goes to his office. When he reaches his office there is a written report waiting for the corps commander. That's what you just asked me about. It's waiting for him on his desk. It's a far more detailed report. He first takes the report and reads it. Having read the report, he notes all positive elements and if there is anything he feels is negative, he makes notes on the document and issues instructions as to what should be done in order to deal with any weaknesses or any problems that have arisen over the last 24 hours. And having read the report, the corps commander usually if one starts working at 8.00, at half past nine -- at half past 8.00 or 9.00 the corps commander gathers his assistants from the corps command. This depends on the structure of the corps command, but there could be seven to ten assistants. They come to his office and this is the morning working meeting and we discuss the daily tasks and duties. We discuss what has been done, what has to be done on that day, and what might have to be done in the future. We discuss tasks that might have to be carried out in the future. So this meeting lasts for at least -- or it lasts for up to one hour. The corps commander issues tasks on the basis of the morning report to all his assistants. If there are any problems that concern morale, legal issues, logistics, he has his assistants for all these sectors and he issues tasks to them so they can remove any shortcomings. And at the end of the working day his assistants gather again. Having read the morning report, the corps commander also has the duty to speak to his immediately subordinate officers. If one starts working at 8.00 or half past 8.00, by 10.00 the corps commander has to be in contact with or rather has to be contacted by all the brigade commanders, or division commanders and OG commanders within the corps. They have to contact him and brief him, report to him about any important matters that might not be contained in the duty officer's report. At the same time that these brigade commanders report to the corps commander, he assigns them certain tasks, gives them certain guidelines as to what they should do on that day, as to what they should do in the near future. Usually after 10.00, when all of this has been dealt with, the corps commander who finds it very difficult to find a day that is not very busy because of all these activities -- well, there are monthly plans that are made, and then from 10.00 to about 2.00 p.m. the corps commander, according to the established plan, is engaged in certain activities. There might be some meetings that have already been organised and certain civilian bodies and it is his duty to attend them. He might have to give lectures, perhaps, as the corps commander, to his units or in cooperation with other bodies. He may be involved in carrying out inspections, controlling the units. He might be involved in drafting plans, documents, short-, mid-term, long-term plans. These are significant duties. He has to plan on what should be done in one year, two years and five years because the corps commander is an operative unit. We continue to use this term, and it's in very close contact with the top military leadership in the state, with the Ministry of the Defence and the Supreme Command who draft these plans. They can't draft these plans without the corps commander. When it comes to drafting these plans, they have the greatest responsibility. A short-term plan is not very problematic. A monthly plan or plan for three or six months or even a one-year plan that -- long term plans for developing or arranging the territory, arming one's self, improving training, et cetera, and education. These are very complex issues and it is necessary to continually study the literature, the documents, foreign and local documents and literature so that a corps commander can deal with all of these issues and keep abreast of military science and military doctrines throughout the world. We all want to follow those who are the best and that is the case today, we're trying to follow the NATO alliance and keep abreast of their developments and certain other -- we're trying to keep abreast of certain other armies in the world, for example the USA army, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's now deal with wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unlike the situation that I have just described, there is also a situation of war. In 90 per cent of the times during the peacetime, the corps commander knows exactly what to do. The corps commander knows in advance what he will be doing every day. The situation, however, is much different during the war, quite contrary to what the commander was doing during the peacetime, for one simple reason. The corps commander during the peacetime, for one simple reason. The corps commander cannot envisage or foresee what might happen the following day and this was especially difficult to do in Bosnia-Herzegovina for a number of reasons. First and foremost most in the war situation there are no working hours. I myself as the corps commander for four years, I slept everywhere else but in my own house. In the four years of war, I did not spend 20 or 30 days at home or I didn't spend 20, 30 nights at home. All the time I slept in my office, because I had a bed there. And if I was not in my office, then I would be in different units and I would sleep in the offices of my subordinate officers, commanders of OGs or commanders of various brigades, or I would sleep in my forward command post. Whenever there were combat operations going on, I would spend a lot of nights under the clear sky in the forest as a corps commander. I repeat, this is not what corps commanders normally do, but in Bosnia this is what all the corps commanders did. And when it comes to describing a day, a typical day of wartime corps commander, I have to say that there are surprise attacks by the enemy which normally starts early in the morning and the main objective of the enemy is to surprise their opponent by such an attack. If I can give you a rough estimate, I would say that out of the four years of the war, at least two years, if not more, every morning I would receive a report on an attack from the east, from the west, or north of Sarajevo; attacks on the lines outside of Sarajevo in Olovo, Fojnica, Tarcin, and so on and so forth. I don't have a map to show these places to you. As soon as a corps commander receives such a report, he gets up immediately and he tries to see how far he is from the place of attack. And, if possible, he tries to establish some sort of communication. In our case, our communication means were -- left a lot to be desired and did not match the communication means of the average, let alone state-of-the-art militaries of the world. First the corps commander tries to establish communication and find out what kind of an attack is going on, and where is it that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. enemy wants to break up the line. The corps commander then reviews the status of his own units, how many of them are close to that sector, how many of them could help the units on the ground. The biggest problem in our units was the fact that we always had very few units in the barracks readily available. We always worked in shifts, in the three shifts that I mentioned. One-third of the men would be on the lines; one-third would be on reserve, if possible; and one-third would be on leave. However, due to the lack of food and accommodation the enemy had destroyed all of our facilities and burned them to the ground and that's why we did not have the facilities to accommodate our men, and that's why we were forced to let our men go and spend the time with their families. In such circumstances it was very difficult to gather our men for a rapid intervention. So let's say in the morning when an attack had started, a fierce attack, a corps commander is in a situation that I am trying to explain; however, it is difficult to put it in words and tell you what really happens in such a situation. If, in such a situation, I was at my main command post in Sarajevo where there were a lot of civilians coming to my office, trying to get a permit to pass through the tunnel to get food for their children and if they didn't get that permit, they would immediately complain to the politicians, complaining about the corps commander who didn't give them the permit. However, I must say that it was not up to the commander to do that. The commander was in charge of those attacks, trying to defend the town. And it was not -- he was not concerned with whether somebody is going to be able to pass through the tunnel and get food. I'm trying to describe the most complex day that I witnessed. Dr. Vahid Kljajic, K-l-j-aj-i-c who is still a professor at the school of political sciences, he -- during the war he was of president of the committee on the distribution of humanitarian aid in Sarajevo. This is humanitarian aid that was air-dropped at the city airport of Sarajevo. At one moment the humanitarian aid channels were interrupted and he reported to me as the corps commander because I cooperated with him very closely. Around 10 o'clock he reported to me that there was no more food and that he couldn't give me anything on that day. My response to him was, how come you can't give him -- me anything? I am just telling you how we spoke. Maybe this is not something that should be said at this level. I told him, doctor, I'm going to kill you. You have to give me food. Later on I had realised that he couldn't give me any because there was none to be had. Then I said to Dr. Kljajic, "I have to be given the last gram of food. If somebody has to starve, it has to be the elderly. The elderly who should be the first to not be given food. It is their turn to die. The last to die is the soldier who is defending the line around the city of Sarajevo." And this is the -- exactly the conversation we had. And also food had to be secured for the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the police. And those were the three bodies that had to be provided with food at all costs. These were the conversations that, in given circumstances, take a toll on any person, that disturb any person's balance and no matter how reasonable a person is, how sensible, all of a sudden you start losing ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's concentrate on typical military problems. During the war, in the -- is there an office where there are maps and similar things from which a corps commander can conduct operations? How -- is there a plan or a map based on which a corps commander can review the situation on the ground? How did you do that during the war?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. At the moment when I said that the corps commander tries to establish communication with the units under attack, he does that from the operation centre. That is, if he is in his main command post. If he is not in his main command post, if he is somewhere else, then he goes to the operation centre or the command post of his subordinate units. And from that place he tries to establish communication through his subordinate officers. He tries to put the situation under control. The first person to be contacted is the brigade commander or two brigade commanders who are in charge of the line through which the enemy is trying to breakthrough. If the situation is very difficult or if the line has already been broken, then the corps commander establishes contacts with other unit commanders and he asks for assistance. Depending on the distance, he orders the units to be engaged in advancing towards that area in order to help those brigade commanders. In doing that he encounters a lot of problems, a lack of fuel, a lack of vehicles and a shortage of troops which would be readily deployable. If he encounters huge problems, multiple problems, which was often the case, then the corps commander has to go to the spot -- the corps commander was expected to do everything, although when you look at it from a human angle, this is not correct. However, a corps commander was expected to do everything. Most of the officers were not trained, were not professionals, were not skillful. They did not have the ability to command their units. They did not have the ability to react quickly, and that is why they tended to pass on the buck upwards to the corps commander. And it was then that the corps commander -- in my case I was on my own in a number of situations, and I had to go directly to the lines 100 metres away from the enemy forces. I would go from one soldier to another to tap them on the shoulder to encourage them to provide them with a guarantee that they would ammunition, food, and reinforcement. What does a corps commander do in such situations? First of all, he contacts his subordinates and asks for them to prevent further advance of the enemy. And when that happens, either on that day or on some of the following days, because the attack may last for seven or ten days, after that there is a continuous activity, a daily activity in order to prepare new troops, quality troops that would engage in a counter attack in order to regain the territory that might have been lost during the attack. When we're talking about- --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment, if you realised that there are problems in communication with the brigade commanders, either because of the problems with the communications or you have problems between yourself and the brigade, what do you do at that moment?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In normal circumstances, such a brigade commander would have everything at his disposal and, in such a case, the corps commander would have a much easier time. However, in Bosnia, every corps commander knew that no brigade commander had the minimum that was required in terms of communication means, ammunition, weapons, equipment, food, and so on and so forth. A corps commander should be in the position to say to his subordinate: You are a brigade commander. You should deal with it. Full stop. However, please, two-thirds -- or up to 1994 most of the brigade commanders in the entire BiH army were people who were self-appointed to that duty and I can claim with full responsibility here that there was a formal accountability in the chain of command. However, if the brigade commander received an order from the corps commander, and if that order was contrary to his views and understanding, he did not carry out that order. And I, as the corps commander in that situation would be faced with the problem whether to remove such a brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you inspected documents from the 3rd Corps, did you face this type of problem when the corps commander might have had problems with his brigade commanders? Did you establish that in the 3rd Corps? I'm not talking about your corps, about the 1st Corps. Did you come across any such problems when you were studying documents from the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did. One of the documents that the commander of the 3rd Corps, General Hadzihasanovic, when he was appointed to that duty -- in one of his reports that he sent to the General Staff -- I could locate this document for you and you would see for yourself that this document illustrates my words very well. He's saying in this document that he could not command over the brigades that already existed. He speaks about the influence of the civilian structures on the brigade commanders and brigade commanders tended to listen to the civilian structures more than to the corps commander, because he could get food from them. He says in this document that there are a lot of people in Bosnia called Celo and Caco. Celo and Caco, I believe that I spoke about these two people against whom I instituted measures on the 26th of October 1996 in order to place them under my command and Caco was executed at that point in time. And I believe that this document was issued towards the he had of November, beginning of December 1992. And in this document General Hadzihasanovic speaks about a number of such people existing in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He says in this document that it was very difficult for him to link up all of his units, because he didn't have the communication means. He didn't have enough officers. The officers that were scent to him by the General Staff From Sarajevo were sent to him because somebody wanted to get rid of them. And when they arrived in Zenica, General Hadzihasanovic could not use them for anything. They did not have qualifications. They didn't have skills. They didn't have any knowledge to be officers. I have just tried to summarize one report that runs over two pages. There are many similar documents in which General Hadzihasanovic reported of such and similar problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the difficulties that you have just explained, between the corps commanders, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th, did you meet amongst yourselves or, given the situation of war, you did not have the possibility to meet or maybe you just contacted over the telephone. How did that go?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to August 1993 we never met. And the main reason for that was the fact that the tunnel had not been broken through under the Sarajevo airport. Once this tunnel was constructed, I could leave Sarajevo, although I did that even before the tunnel. I ran across the runway, against the express orders of UNPROFOR. They shot after me, but I had to leave Sarajevo in order to save Mount Igman, I-g-m-a-n, in the vicinity of Sarajevo. This was in the summer of 1993 and the tunnel was broken through on the first of August 1993. Before then, none of us corps commanders met. After August 1993, up to the end of the war, from time to time we did have meetings of corps commanders. Up to the end of 1995, there might have been four, five, or six such meetings. I don't know exactly how many. But the 5th corps commander was never there. He could never attend such meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Let's move to the Main Staff. You said you were in Sarajevo and the other corps commanders were not there. And how did the Main Staff have contacts with them? Was it done by telephone, by courier, by fax? As far as you know, how did the Main Staff establish contacts with other corps commanders?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war in 1992, it's very difficult to say how it managed to maintain communications. The communications equipment used was very poor and there were various types of communications equipment used. However, later on during the last three years of the war, we tried to establish repeaters, the dominant features of the most elevated points that were under our control. And we used Paket communications. And that means communicating by a computer system. We had our own special codes to ensure that the enemy could not intercept our communications and decrypt our communications. And later, this means of communications functioned quite well. But this was the highest level of communication. When we're talking about the communication between the Main Staff and the corps commanders. But the corps commander didn't have such communications with his OGs, his operative groups. This form of communication is expensive and we didn't have sufficient men who were capable of using such systems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know did the Main Staff have good -- a good level of control over the corps commanders? I'm not talking about you, but with regard to corps commanders who were outside the town. For example in the 3rd Corps, did the Main Staff have a good view of activities of the corps? What do you think about this?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first say my main command post was in Sarajevo. But at the same time, the main command post of the Main Staff was in Sarajevo because that was requested by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The forward command post, my forward command post, and the Main Staff forward command post, after the tunnel in Sarajevo had been made, when Visoko and in certain other places, in Kakanj, and a certain number of officers were deployed from the central -- from the main command post to the forward command posts the Presidency made the following requests. When the commander of the Main Staff was in Sarajevo, had to be outside of Sarajevo. If I was outside of Sarajevo then the command of the Main Staff had to be in Sarajevo. That was one request. But when you mentioned the issue of control, I can provide you with an example. It's difficult for me to say how much control they had. At the beginning, after I had been arrested in Tuzla on the 27th of April 1992 and after I had been taken to Belgrade, I was replaced by Colonel Zeljko Knez as commander of the district staff or soon afterwards as commander of the 2nd of the ABiH. He was appointed naturally by the Presidency by the minister of defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He's a Croat, the commander -- a corps commander in the ABiH. In 1992, things went smoothly. I don't know when he transferred his duties in 1993. When he handed over his duties, it seemed that communications between the Main Staff commander and the 2nd Corps commander were functioning adequately. However, later, we found out that Zeljko Knez was in direct contact with Franjo Tudjman and there is evidence to support this. And he did contribute to the defence of north-eastern Bosnia. Things should have been done in a different way. That came to light after on. Later, Zeljko Knez after he had handed over his duties as corps commander, was replaced because people realised that things weren't going well. And in the background he seemed to be working for the interests of Franjo Tudjman. He fled to Croatia and never returned to Bosnia again. So I'm just providing you with an example to describe the situation. All other commanders were Bosniaks. There were Serbs and Croats at lower levels, there were commanders, et cetera, but not that many. Those corps commanders and naturally with the 2nd Corps commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to focus on the Main Staff again. Could you tell us, again, the name of the supreme commander that you were in contact with.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the Chief of Staff, Hasan Efendic, the chief of the Territorial Defence Staff, and then towards the end of May 1992 his duties were taken over by Sefer Halilovic. And on the 8th of June, 1993, Rasim Delic took over the duties of Sefer Halilovic and he remained in that position until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The supreme commander, from June, was Delic. Did he have daily contact with his corps commanders, over the phone, was there daily contact between the supreme commander and his corps commanders?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to many of the rules he should have had daily contact with them. However, and I'm telling you about my own case, I didn't have daily contact. However, the longest period during which I had no contact with the supreme commander was two or three days, unless he left Bosnia-Herzegovina because of certain tasks. But then I would have contact with his deputies. Why didn't I contact the commander of the Main Staff every day? Because I could never obtain anything from him. It's difficult to put it in this way. It's difficult to say I could never obtain anything from him, but I couldn't obtain the quantity of weapons and ammunition that I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. needed especially in 1992 and 1993. In the same part of 1994 and in 1995 the situation somewhat improved. In the course of 1992 and 1993, and partly in 1994, too, the Main Staff was more or less completely excluded from plans for combat activities. It was the corps who were mostly engaged in planning combat activities. They lived in the territory. They would feed themselves in that territory and they would obtain supplies from the territory they were in. The situation was such that the corps commanders had to act in an independent manner to a significant extent. However, a corps commander never refused to obey an order from the Main Staff commander, because these people were all officers. All the corps commanders had come from the JNA and they were well aware of what it meant to be a good commander, a good officer, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to go to a superior level. As a Ministry of Defence above the supreme commander, who was the Ministry of Defence in 1992 -- in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I know the exact dates. The first minister of Defence was Jerko Doko, in 1992, at the beginning of the war. Then, he was succeeded by -- I don't know if he was the ministry or deputy minister, he was always a Bosniak or Croat, I can't remember his name. For a certain period of time there was has Hasan Cengic. I don't know if he was the minister or deputy minister. I'm not sure. That was in 1993. And then there was someone from Visoko, whose name was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the commander of the 1st Corps, were you visited by the minister of the defence? Did he go and visit you in the field? Because you yourself said that you would go to the lines to encourage the soldiers. Did the minister of defence visit you to see what you were doing and to see what the situation was like? Did you meet the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff would appear. The minister of defence, never a single minister of defence throughout the war ever went to visit any part of the army and I can tell you the Ministry of Defence is also a sort of superior command, not my direct superior command, but it's an indirect superior command at another level and I had no particular form of contact with the Ministry of Defence, absolutely none. Because it's difficult for me to say this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking you this question because in your report, in paragraph 282 you mentioned the principle of subordination of militaries with respect to the government. That is paragraph 282. And further on in paragraph 287, you said that the exercise of command by generals was carried out under the control of the Presidency and of the Supreme Command. You have just said that the minister of defence is someone that you yourself never met, never saw. So how was political control exercised over military bodies that, according to you, were controlled by civilian and political bodies? How did the Presidency establish control, exercise control if they never went into the field? Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: A while ago I said that the Ministry of Defence never went into the field. But the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina did. On countless occasions, Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, visited the units of my corps. He came to my corps command and even went to the front line in the vicinity, he even went to the front line or a few hundred metres from the front line and he even went to the front line itself, at the Zuc feature in Sarajevo. He went to visit the soldiers in the first trenches. And I can claim that that was also the case with the second member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mirko Pejanovic. He also went to the corps command on countless occasions. He didn't go to the front line that often but he did that on a couple of occasions too. And the Croat, the third member of the Presidency, Kljujic also did that on a few occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. President Izetbegovic visited you on a number of occasions. As part of your responsibilities as the corps commander, did you feel that the supreme political authority was perfectly well informed of what was happening in the field?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. I wouldn't say that they were perfectly well informed. Had they been perfectly well informed, they wouldn't have come to visit the unit. The reason for such visits was usually to discover what the situation was like in the units, to find out the truth about the situation. The Supreme Command was perhaps informed in general terms with regard to the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and its relation to international bodies. But as to the situation at the front lines in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Supreme Command came to such information through the Main Staff. Very often groups of various people were formed. There would be a member of the Presidency at its head and they would then go to visit units, or rather the corps, especially in 1994 and 1995, there would be members of the Main Staff with them and there would be the corps commanders and his assistants, there were such visits. The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the supreme commander of the army had contact with the prime minister. The prime minister did his work in the sense that he would supply or obtain food for the army, for the civilians. But as far as military issues are concerned, the Supreme Command had contact with the command of the Main Staff and the Main Staff had contact with the corps commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that information. I would now like to go down to the level of operations in the field. There are a number of situations. We have offensive operations, defensive operations or operations to hold the lines facing the enemy. So we have various situations. If there is an event, if for example the enemy attacks the unit in the field which is engaged in military terms by the enemy, how does it draft a report on the situation for its superior. Can you tell us how information is circulated in such situations and how information is forwarded up the chain of command? Let's take a basic unit, part of a company is attacked by the enemy. What happens in such a case?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about a minor attack by the enemy. In such an attack, the platoon commander, if his platoon was attacked he will report to his company commander, because there is no way for him to report to anybody else. The company commander reports to the battalion commander. It was very uncommon for a company commander to be able to report to somebody else, save for his head of municipality, and there are such cases especially during the first months of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the attack is of a large scale rather than a minor attack, which might result in the line being broken through, and if there is danger facing other units as well, will the corps commander be aware -- made aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the attack is of a larger scale, which means that an entire brigade has been attacked or even more than one brigade, then this is a very serious situation and the corps commander has to be informed about such a situation because this will require a much bigger engagement of all the parts of the corps. The attack in this case involves a bigger line and engages more than one brigade. The corps commander will then alert his entire chain of command, all of his subordinates and he has to start thinking at the operational level. For example, if this happened in Turbe near Travnik in the area of the 3rd Corps, for example if Travnik and Bugojno have come under attack, the corps commander immediately has to start thinking where another attack may ensue. Because when the enemy launches an attack, it will not happen only on one axis. The attack will be gradual and it will attempt to engage the entire 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's talk about a different situation. For example, the corps is engaged in an offensive operation. The corps starts moving forward in order to take the positions which are occupied by the enemy, again we're talking about a large-scale operation. At which moment, at the end of the operation, is the -- the outcome of the operation evaluated?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment when the person who issued the order to start the attack or assault, when that person issues an order to stop such an operation, this is when the evaluation starts. Depending on the scale of this attack, which may last anything between a couple of hours to a couple of weeks, when this stops and the attack has to be stopped at one point, then the results are evaluated in terms of the success of this operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The evaluation of the results, is it done in a direct contact between the corps commander and commanders of his brigades?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less this is how it's done. After the end of such an attack, the corps commander gathers a number of his assistants and commanders of the units which participated in the attack. And they are gathered. There is a debriefing. And the debriefing will go along these lines: I started the attack at this and that hour. The attack lasted for two hours. I took certain facilities. I took a certain line. And there are also assistants who follow all that and they enter all that information into the maps which exist in the operation centre. I had problems and finally the commanders who participated in the attack will come forth with some requests. For example, I request a certain number of additional men because I had so many dead and wounded. I request replenishment of food, ammunition, fuel and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is collateral damage during the attack, if there are civilian casualties, would such collateral damage be assessed and would the corps commander ask about the sources of such collateral damage, or not? When I say "collateral damage," I mean houses that had been torched, shells falling where they shouldn't have fallen, civilians who were killed during the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, yes. If collateral damage has been noticed and recorded, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would move on to another problem. When there were foreigners, volunteers, people who came from Arabic and African countries according to you were the foreigners, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, people who came from all over the place in order to help the BiH army, did you, in your corps, have anybody from abroad that served in the area of your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my corps, I didn't have any such people. Anybody carrying arms, anybody engaged in any shape or form together with my units, under my command, no. I didn't have such men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what about other corps? Did you have any information about the possibility of foreigners being on the strength of other units? For example, a witness testified here - and I am speaking from memory - this witness said there was a Russian doctor who was a member of a unit. Were there foreigners who might have been engaged in the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that you have put this second question to me, I can tell that I was not correct in my first answer. When I said that there were no such men in my corps I men that there were no larger groups, there were no groups of five, ten, or larger groups of such men. I did have one case in my corps, however, in 1992, a German came, either through UNPROFOR or I don't know how. He was a German who came to Sarajevo and he became a member of the 102nd motorised brigade in Stup, S-t-u-p, in the western part of Sarajevo and he fought as a foot soldier for a year and after that he was killed and we know exactly where his grave is in Sarajevo. These were individual cases to which I don't assign any significance. What I meant when I gave you my first answer was that there are no larger groups of such men. There are no larger groups of men of that sort in the 1st, 2nd, or 4th, or 5th Corps the only exception being the 3rd corps, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On several occasions you mentioned the issue of weapons. In your report in paragraph 104 you mention the types of weapons that existed in the JNA. For example, you mentioned tanks, and you say that the JNA had 2.100 tanks, 2.000 pieces of artillery pieces and so on and so forth. In paragraph 331 of your report, again you are talking about weapons and you mention weapons in paragraph 111. However, in your report we did not come across a precise figure, or no figure at all about the weaponry at the disposal of the BiH army. Could you just briefly tell us whether the BiH army had tanks as far as you know? Did you have tanks?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just give you a brief introduction and then I will move on to tanks. When it comes to the JNA weaponry, I used certain sources and I also used sources when I spoke about the BiH army. I don't know whether this information is precise, whether these sources were accurate. Secondly, the BiH army was on my mind when I was preparing this report and I did have an overview of the BiH army weapons, and I took the year 1993 as an example, and I also singled out a 3rd Corps. However, it is very difficult for me to give you any of the figures off my head. Now, tanks. The BiH army did have tanks. However, if we look at the situation in different corps, the 1st Corps which had over 70 or 75.000 men, throughout the entire war I had no more than five tanks. The -- and I also captured seven new tanks towards the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were no more than five?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three could be used. Two could never be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will come back to that in a minute. In paragraph 369 you are talking about the problem of the fifth column. What is the fifth column?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Historically speaking, the fifth column first came about during the Second World War, if not before. And historically speaking I believe that the history books say that the fifth column first came into existence in the former Yugoslavia north of Belgrade. And at that time the fifth column implied people who collaborated directly with the Nazi troops. And this notion still exists in Bosnia and Herzegovina, when we say the fifth column, we mean people, groups of people or individuals who collaborate with the enemy and who can be found in the area of responsibility of the BiH army or under the control of various corps of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last time when we had a map or a relief at our disposal in the courtroom, you explained what the situation was on the ground. And in my view the situation was very complicated and complex. At one point you told us that there was a man whose name was Fikret Abdic. Who is that man? What did he represent what is he a threat what kind of threat was he? It was then that we heard, for the first time his name. It was the first time for me to hear his name. Who is that person, Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to be very brief and up to the point. Fikret Abdic was a person who was engaged in politics before the war. At the very beginning of the war, in the elections that took place in 1990, he got a majority of votes and he was supposed to be elected in place of Alija Izetbegovic. When Alija Izetbegovic was captured in Lukavica near Sarajevo, as he was returning from negotiations abroad, at that moment he wanted to carry out a putsch in the state. His intention was to keep Bosnia and Herzegovina in the greatest Serbia, although he is a Muslim, Bosniak by ethnic origin. After that, he was eliminated from the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He returned to his native Krajina, which is the north-western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the name of the place is Velika Kladusa in the north-western part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Before the war, he was a prominent person in his area. He was a well-known businessman. Since he didn't agree with Alija Izetbegovic and his policies, he, as a Bosniak Muslim, established his own army which consisted of Bosniaks and Muslims and he proclaimed this part of territory his own autonomous region called Western Bosnia. I'm referring to the north-western part that was coloured Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. differently in one of my annexes. This was in the area of responsibility of the 5th Corps of the BiH army, which was headquartered in Bihac. Fikret Abdic directly collaborated with Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade and Franjo Tudjman in Zagreb. He had direct contacts with the two of them, and he worked directly with the army of the Republika Srpska and the HVO. He established an army, as I already told you, and he had several thousand troops. I don't know how many. Maybe even more than I think he did. During the year 1993, when there was fighting in Central Bosnia with the HVO and the Republika Srpska army, he also activated his troops in Krajina and he wanted to be become the third enemy to the BiH army. I can tell you that when he was engaged in fighting against the 5th Corps of the BiH army, several thousand men got killed on both sides. Fikret Abdic had also established camps, detainee camps. After the war, when the war was over, he moved to Croatia. He took Croatian citizenship and he did that with the support of the Croatian president Franjo Tudjman. There were criminal charges against him by The Hague Tribunal, and The Hague Tribunal then agreed that Fikret Abdic should be tried in Croatia, in Karlovac. A few years ago he was sentenced to a prison sentence of 20 years. And a few months ago, there was another hearing on appeal and I believe that his sentence was reduced from 20 years to 15 years in prison. And currently he is serving his prison sentence in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is 10.32, we shall have our first break. After the break I will have only two more questions and then I will give the floor to the parties. We shall resume at around 11 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few more questions, but we should be able to proceed very rapidly. General, in paragraph 312 you mentioned the fact that the command post, the forward command post of the Supreme Command at Mount Igman had opinion captured. That is in paragraph 312. With regard to forward command posts, could you tell us how many elements it contains. Is the forward command post positioned as close as possible to the enemy and is the purpose of a forward command post the possibility of obtaining relevant information, is that the purpose for a forward command post? When the command post at Mount Igman was captured, where was it transferred? And secondly, can you describe a command post for us, how many men did it consist of and could you provide us with any other relevant information.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question in fact contains the answer. Most of the answer is implicit in your question. A forward command post, any command at any level forms a forward command post for the reasons that you have just mentioned in your question. The main reasons for forming a forward command post are as follows: To approach, to have a certain number of officers from the command in the vicinity of the front line in order to see what the situation is, how the situation develops and in order to control all the combat activities in that area, in the area covered by the forward command post. The senior officer to forward command post usually has direct contact with the commander of the unit representing him at the forward command post. If the corps commander establishes a forward command post, then the command of the forward command post is in direct contact with the corps commander. Since in paragraph 312 I mentioned one such command post in 1992 on Mount Igman, in military terms it should be just a forward command post, but in terms of the number of men and in terms of the way in which this group of three officers operated, it would be difficult to claim that this was in fact a forward command post because a forward command post requires more men. You need at least one officer from each sector, from each body of the corps command, if the corps command is deploying a forward command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My penultimate question, which is rather long. If necessary, note down the paragraphs I'm going to quote. This question will be almost as long as the questions put to you by Mr. Bourgon, but I don't think that it will be longer than his questions. Paragraph 625. You mentioned three events, Totic's kidnapping in April in 1993. Six Croats in Miletici who were killed and the kidnapping and murdering of a number of individuals on the 8th of June 1993. Individuals who had been escorted by the 306th brigade. That is what you said in paragraph 625. Paragraph 629, in that paragraph you explained that the corps commander was not responsible for the activities of individuals or groups of individuals. Further on, you explained what the corps commander had to do. In paragraph 634, you said that the corps commander had to obtain as much information as possible on individuals, weapons, resources, et cetera. In paragraph 635 you said that the corps commander had to inform his superiors of the presence of these individuals. In paragraph 639, you also said that if the activities of such individuals had an affect on the corps's mission, the commander had to consult his superior command and take measures to deal with the problem that had arisen. With regard to these events Totic, Miletici, and the 8th of June, 1993, you said, in relation to Totic, in paragraph 644 an order was issued to the military police to cooperate with HVO military police and with the civilian police in Zenica. As far as Miletici is concerned, you said in paragraph 646 that measures were taken in order to obtain information on their activities and you said that the corps commander had informed the Supreme Command at a meeting. As far as Maline is concerned, in paragraph 647 you said that on the 13th of June General Hadzihasanovic wrote a report and forwarded it to the Supreme Command, a report in which the presence of the Mujahedin was mentioned. And you said that he received an order to disarm them or to send them to Mount Igman. So my question is as follows: With regard to these three events, Totic, the five Croats in Miletici and the people who were kidnapped on the 8th of June 1993, you said in your report - and perhaps this is something you referred to elsewhere too, but I would like to hear about this - you said that at no point in time was the intervention of the civilian authorities mentioned as a possibility. The civilian authorities were not involved in these three events, with the exception perhaps of Totic, in which case the civilian police conducted an investigation with the military police. But in two other cases the civilian authorities are not referred to. Did you simply fail to mention them? Is this an omission? Or is this a result of certain other circumstances? How is it that the civilian authorities were not mentioned in your report? Could you provide us with an explanation of any kind. And in your zone of responsibility, did you ever have contact with the civilian authorities in order to conduct investigations into certain events, certain activities? How would you analyse situation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the events when the civilian authorities intervened or the civilian police, these events have been mentioned and enumerated, that's a positive example. And it's good in terms of the way in which the overall social system functioned or rather defence system in the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the case of the events where no reference was made to this or when there was only a brief reference, well, for example, in Mehurici there was a forward civilian police station, if I may call it in that way, that in fact it was just there as a passive observer. In other events there is no reference to such bodies, since this was never the case. It was only subsequently, if commissions were formed in someone from the civilian organs or bodies participated as a member in the commission when the consequences of certain events were subsequently established, either in Miletici or Maline. And that's where the problem lies. There were foreigners, such as they were, and the 3rd Corps of the ABiH had no power over them, was not responsible for them and they were present in the territory of the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. But I said that the entire territory was not covered by the corps. So it's not only that they weren't responsible for the appearance of these foreigners, but they also weren't responsible for the civilian police or the civilian protection or for the political bodies that were there, et cetera, et cetera. On the other hand, the civilian authorities, those who had political power, and those who were in control of the civilian police were more or less passive in relation to foreign combatants. The question is, why? If I tried to answer the question I might be biased because I don't have reliable information and I don't have such information because I still don't know who these foreigners were, where they came from, what their real names were, what their objective was, why they had come to Bosnia-Herzegovina, what they wanted, who sent them, and where they are today, at least most of them. To this very day, this is still a riddle throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and beyond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that answer. My last question is as follows: A number of witnesses who have appeared here before you mentioned that there were investigations that had been successfully conducted that related to individuals who handed themselves over to the commission for violations. The witnesses mentioned three examples. One concerns the green league, there were members of the 314th brigade, elements from the 7th brigade, that were part of what one witness called "the mountain guerilla," and reference was also made to the "Turkish guerilla." Foreigners who had handed themselves over for the Commission for Crimes or Misdemeanours, and the witnesses told us the military police, thanks to the investigations carried out and thanks to the military logistics, made it possible for these individuals to be arrested, especially members of the Turkish guerilla who were apparently individuals carrying arms and they were neutralised. In response to a question you said that the army was not capable of carrying out military operations against the Mujahedin. It was not in a position to do that. But you yourself, at the head of the 1st Corps, you said that you carried out an operation, a military operation against two brigades or the leaders of two brigades. So my question is as follows, in purely military terms, leaving aside all political or other considerations, in purely military terms, in 1993, was the ABiH in a position to neutralise 10 or 100 individuals if these individuals only had light arms, rifles, assault rifles, revolvers of various kinds, et cetera. Did the ABiH, or was the ABiH capable of neutralising such individuals, or not. It seems a few days ago you said this was not possible. In military terms could you tell us whether it was possible, or not. And a minute ago you also said that the army had five tanks. Everyone knows the sort of damage that a tank can cause. So in military terms, was it possible for the army to neutralise these individuals, or not? Or was the problem of an entirely different kind?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very complex question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I have put it to you.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, if I may reply briefly by saying that I was not exclusive when I said that the ABiH army could not institute measures against the foreigners. I said that under the circumstances it would have been very difficult for the 3rd Corps or the army to do that. I did not rule out that possibility completely, as you have put it. In order to be very clear, let me say this. During the year 1993, the BiH army had five corps and I will repeat the first one was in Sarajevo, the second one in Tuzla, the third one in Zenica, the fourth in Mostar, and the fifth in Bihac. Up to the year 1994, that is the summer of 1994, there was no possibility whatsoever and there was no cooperation or assistance between the various corps of the BiH army. This is a very important fact. This was not possible for several reasons, and such a cooperation was not in place. It was only in the summer 1994 and throughout 1995 when the conditions were put in place for one corps assisting another corps by way of resubordination of some of its units. In 1993, this was not feasible. This was not possible. And it wasn't done. I am saying this because we are dealing with the notion of the BiH army and now we're talking only about the 3rd Corps and the zone of responsibility of this corps and its units. This corps could not have been assisted by anybody in the year 1993. They could not have been assisted with a single soldier, a single rifle, a single tank. Secondly, you said that the BiH army had five or seven tanks. It was not the army. My corps had the tanks, that's what I said in my answer. We had five tanks, three of which could be used and I captured the additional seven towards the end of 1994. The tanks that I had at my disposal in 1993, three usable and five on the stock, they were in the town of Sarajevo. And they did not mean a thing to the 3rd Corps. They could not leave Sarajevo. I don't know how many tanks the 3rd Corps had. Very few, I presume. A couple maybe. And I'm not taking into account any of the other armourment. Whatever there was, it was not available to the 3rd Corps. And as for the 3rd Corps and its overall situation that prevailed and I tried to explain to you, with the use of the map, the relief, and the slides that I showed to you, illustrates the most difficult year when they had to man lines facing the Republika Srpska army, when they had a number of Croatian enclaves within its zone of responsibility, when it had a large fifth column in its zone of responsibility and, on top of that, they had Fikret Abdic in Western Bosnia. What I did in Sarajevo with my two brigades is not important. I was very precise when I said that it was much easier for me to do that because my two brigades in Sarajevo covered two neighbourhoods in the town of Sarajevo. And I knew exactly where the commands of those brigades were, where the commands of their subordinate battalions were, and other units within those brigades and so on and so forth. I had all of that information, all of the information. When I launched an attack, it was in a limited area, in a limited zone. And in addition to that, in Sarajevo, I had enough men. I had even too many men. When the tunnel was made, I could send my men on a daily basis from Sarajevo to fight on the outer circle of Sarajevo. I had many more men in Sarajevo than outside Sarajevo and I was able to do that. However, the command of the 3rd Corps had a different problem. In 1993 his troops were stretched to the maximum and because he was attacked from all sides, and because he had about 400 kilometres of line facing the Republika Srpska army, and the HVO and given the number of troops that he had in his corps, he could not secure his line of defence by deploying one soldier at every ten metres of his defence line, and he could not expect assistance from anybody. In addition to that, there was no cooperation or practically no cooperation between the 3rd Corps and the civilian police. Enver Hadzihasanovic, as the corps commander, had very little information about foreign citizens. He didn't know who they were, where they came from, and where they were located. A group would appear in Mehurici, another one would appear in Miletici, a third one would appear in Zenica. They captured Totic and then another group appeared in Travnik. It was a very complex and complicated situation for a corps commander. A military is an instrument which calls for a clarity of a vision in order to launch an which calls for a clarity, a vision in order to launch an operation. The troops and their commanders are not allowed to embark on any random adventures, so to speak. And, if I may add another sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, engaging a number of military police and special units, companies or platoons in order to arrest them in such a huge area from Zenica to Travnik, this would have called for a lot of energy and a lot of troops without a certain outcome. He wouldn't know how many troops Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. he might have lost. He did not have the approval from the top political echelons like I had in Sarajevo. In Sarajevo, the Supreme Command ordered me to cooperate with the civilian police. He did not have such instructions there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've mentioned the green light by the Supreme Command that you had in Sarajevo. In paragraph 648, you mention an order that was sent by the Supreme Command, either to send the Mujahedin to Mount Igman or to disarm them. What -- was that the green light for an action against them? How would you analyse this order? You saw that order because you mentioned it in paragraph 648. How would you analyse this? Is this the green light? Or is this a pre-order which calls for a military reaction? How would you analyse this document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't have those documents here. I would like to show it to you, but I have it in Sarajevo. The order that I received from the supreme corps and the Main Staff when I was supposed to send out my two brigades on the 26th of October, 1993. This is an entirely different situation to the order that was given to the 3rd Corps commander by the Supreme Command to either disarm foreigners or to send them to Mount Igman. How did I understand this order? My understanding of this order was as follows, and I will try to be very short and up to the point. Why did the Supreme Command issue that order? Because the 3rd Corps commander complained on a number of occasions, and he asked for assistance. He asked for the problems of foreign citizens to be resolved by civilian police, primarily. However, this did not bear any fruit. He put it on paper as well, although he didn't do it willingly, I suppose. Because he wrote about something that was not part of his mission and still it posed him a lot of problem in carrying out his mission. Due to the lack of information about foreign citizens that one should have had in order to deal with that problem, in the document that the 3rd Corps commander sent to the Main Staff there is a lack of information based on that scarce information the 3rd Corps commander -- the supreme commander sent this document to the 3rd Corps commander. The document that you're talking about. That's how I analyse it. The problem of foreign citizens was not taken seriously, I believe. Not because the commander of the Main Staff was not serious, but because nobody had the exact information as to how the -- how serious the problem was in the first place. I said the other day that this order looked to me as a formal order and it was drafted in that sense by the commander of the Main Staff. He ordered the 3rd Corps commander to disarm those people or to send them to Igman. I see this like a situation when two people meet each other or come across each other at a traffic light and they don't have the time to discuss an issue at great length, so they say something to each other just passing by. He probably believed that there were very few such people, but that was not the case. In addition to that, the commander of the Main Staff should not have taken upon himself the responsibility of issuing such a document. He should have asked the Supreme Command to do that or the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He should have waited for them to issue an order to the civilian police and to himself, and then the civilian police with the security service of the 3rd Corps should have gathered enough information, they should have located these people and so on and so forth. And after that the order should have been issued and the action should have been launched to eliminate that. However, this would have been a lengthy process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer. I'm now going to ask the Prosecution if they wish to ask any additional questions and then I'm going to give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We do have a few additional questions that arise from those put by Your Honour to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, earlier this morning reflected at page 14, lines 3 and 4 of the transcript, you were answering a question about the quality of, or the level of training and professionalism of soldiers in the ABiH. And part of your answer was as follows: "Most of the officers were not trained, were not professionals, were not skillful." And my question to you, sir, is: Would you include General Hadzihasanovic as being among the officers who were not trained, not professional, and not skilled?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would you include Brigadier Kubura among the officers who were not professional, not trained, or not skillful?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't, but just a little remark. Both of them were relatively young for the positions that they held. They had enough knowledge that they acquired in the previous army. I would have to calculate to see how old Brigadier Kubura was when he was appointed the brigade commander. I believe that he was in his 30s. He was very young. In the previous army, for somebody to become a brigade commander under the age of 40, it was not possible. And the same goes for General Hadzihasanovic. And in that sense, they did lack certain experience for command activities and I was the same case. I am even younger than General Hadzihasanovic, but I'm talking about them. This is what we lacked. We lacked experience, but we gained experience in practice, so to speak. I was talking generally and I said "no" because all of us officers were formed and trained in the BiH army. And the officers, like me, they're only about two and a half per cent in the entire BiH army and if I, as the corps commander, was an ideal professional, but if all the other of my officers were not the same, then I, at the top, would mean very -- very -- would mean very little, because I as an individual without the support of my subordinate officers, could not do anything on my own. Let me give you an example. I had two brigade commanders in Sarajevo, in Dobrinja, D-o-b-r-i-n-j-a, and later on one of the brigade commanders in Hrasnica became a division commander in Sarajevo when I established three divisions in my corps. One of my divisions was in Sarajevo and two were outside of Sarajevo. This person in Sarajevo, Fikret Prevljak, and the brigade commander of that division in Sarajevo Ismet Hadzic, were civilians. One of them was a policeman before the war he was Fikret Prevljak, and Ismet Hadzic was a religious official before the war. They had only secondary school degrees. At the beginning of the war, they proved themselves to be very good fighters and they were able to lead the troops in the defence of the town. The brigades were formed and later on I had problems with them when I gave them command positions because they could not carry out my orders precisely. And they had direct contacts with the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina or some other people. They bypassed me. In 1995, at one point, they made such a huge mistake that I, as the corps commander, decided to remove them from their respective positions. Both Fikret Prevljak and Ismet Hadzic, as division commander and brigade commander respectively, and I did that with the approval of Rasim Delic. And I instituted criminal proceedings against both of them with the military district court in Sarajevo. At the same time I issued an order appointing people as acting commanders until the moment I was able to appoint new commanders. Two days later President Izetbegovic requested that my order should be made null and void, my order on their removal from their respective positions. On the order of President Izetbegovic, General Delic made my decision null and void, because he could do that. He had the right to do that. They were returned to their respective duties. However, the criminal proceedings that I instituted with the military district court could not be made null and voided, because it was within my exclusive purview. And in order for this to be made null and void and for them not to be prosecuted by the military district I had to be removed from my position of the corps commander and this was done a month later. And which I was replaced by a new commander, he then decided to cancel the criminal proceedings before the military district court. I'm just giving you one example which is corroborated by all the relevant documents in the archives of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Karavelic, I appreciate that answer and I also the example you've given. Sir, I think all of us here in the courtroom would like to get you back home as quickly as possible, so I'm going to ask you if you could try to keep the answers as short as possible, because once I'm done both of the defence teams will have a further opportunity. And if -- if -- if we need an example, I will certainly ask you if you can recall an example. But let me ask you this, with respect to the situation in the 3rd Corps. You have -- both in your written report and in your testimony, you have demonstrated the extremely complex and extremely difficult conditions that existed in the 3rd Corps during 1993. Let me ask you this, sir. Did the situation, during 1993, in Central Bosnia, in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility, did the situation completely collapse?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very good question, if I may say so. In my view, in the summer of 1993, the situation in Central Bosnia was such as it was and it ended at the top of the pyramid of the state in both political and military terms. I'm talking about an Egyptian pyramid and I am talking about its top, and it was just a matter of time or a new political or military event for the situation to change for the better, or for the disappearance of the BiH army and the Bosnian state. Luckily enough the situation changed for the better, or started changing for the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I guess that's my point, General.
