The fact that the corps had the 3rd Corps had, as you've told us, some officers who weren't fully trained who lacked experience, who lacked certain skills, the fact of the matter is that the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not collapse during 1993 and they were successful in defending that territory and holding that territory throughout 1993, notwithstanding the fact that within that corps there were individuals who lacked experience, who lacked professional training, and who lacked the requisite military skills that one would have hoped for in a peacetime corps structure and organisation. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, this is close to my way of thinking. But there were two reasons for that, two key reasons for that. The first one is the fact that these people, these officers starting with the corps commander and other people in the chain of command, who were aware of the situation and who were aware that this was the top of the pyramid, that this was the make or break of the situation, they worked around the clock and working around the clock they could put as many as 72 hours into the 24 hours that they worked. They made huge sacrifices. They worked very hard and that is the case. I'm not being biased when I say that, because this is not the case. The case is what I'm talking about. And the second reason is the fact that the 3rd Corps, at that time realised that it was at the top of the pyramid and that it decided to embark on the process to re sol of the situation with the HVO. If this had not been done, if it did not create the real situation with the HVO, if they hadn't asked them whether they were the enemy or an ally, and if this had not been done in Central Bosnia, if the situation had not been clarified, if the new lines of defence facing the HVO and the Republika Srpska army had not been established, and they should have been only so lucky to be able to do that with the foreigners, and that is when the situation started changing for the better, gradually, step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But again sir my only point is, that the 3rd Corps, despite all the problems and despite all the complexities, the 3rd Corps held its ground. The territory in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility did not, for the most part, fall into the hands of either the HVO or the VRS in 1993.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent. In one of my annexes a few days ago I mentioned the objective of the Republika Srpska army in 1993 and the objective of the HVO, and you may have seen in one of the annexes when one of the colours changes into another colour. The Republika Srpska army in the course of 1993 took upon itself the task to act together with the HVO and to focus on eastern Bosnia on the entire eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the south to the north, from Bijeljina and down to Dubrovnik, to Trebinje. And that is what they did. And as you have seen in the course of 1993, you saw how much territory the Republika Srpska army occupied in the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. How much territory they took from the ABiH? They took a lot of territory. And they turned Gorazde and Zepa and Srebrenica into enclaves in the course of 1993. And we reached an agreement with the HVO, they said "the HVO should operate in the central part of Bosnia because we share the same objective." And the HVO tried to do this in central part of Bosnia. And the credit should be given to the 3rd Corps commander for having recognised the fact, so the Republika Srpska army didn't attack the 3rd Corps to a significant extent because they had taken their forces to eastern Bosnia and they were only holding lines towards the 3rd Corps here. Because the HVO was to focus in on the territory of Central Bosnia and the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps and that is why I'm saying that credit should be given to the 3rd Corps commander for having acted without decision from the state leadership and in order to deal with the situation. And they were very successful in dealing with the sayings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just to follow up from the end of your last answer, you said "credit should be given to the 3rd Corps commander for having acted without decision from the state leadership and in order to deal with the situation." Isn't that kind of autonomous, if you will, action; the type of thing one would expect from a corps commander? Not to have to wait for direction from the leadership?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: When someone is to die, when someone drowns in a river or is drowning in a river and is struggling to obtain enough oxygen to survive, well I wouldn't say that that was the situation, but the situation was similar to that kind of a situation. The political and military leadership in April of 1992 said the HVO is an integral part of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The HVO said "we won't recognize the Territorial Defence and the armed forces of the legal government, the legal state of Bosnia and Herzegovina." In spite of that fact, in August 1992 President Izetbegovic went to see Tudjman in Zagreb, went to see the president of the Republic of Croatia. And together they reached an agreement and Tudjman was allegedly to order the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina to participate as a separate component on an equal footing with the ABiH, and they were to form the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- they were to be under the control of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I think that there is even a legal document to that effect. However, these were just empty promises. And in fact it was an attempt on the part of the Croatian leadership to gain time. Later on, the leaders in Bosnia-Herzegovina felt that they could not declare that Croatia or the HVO was an aggressor because then the political leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the ABiH would have been encircled, fully encircled. And it would only have been a matter of days as to when the army and the political leadership and the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina would disappear. So they could never tell the commander of the Main Staff or the 3rd Corps commander that as of today you should consider the HVO as the aggressor and that you should open fire on them. That was the reason, because there would be -- they would have been acting against their own interest. They would have condemned themselves to death. That is why the 3rd Corps commander continually strove to avoid a conflict with the HVO. He did everything that he could to avoid such a conflict. He didn't want to open fire on them, although they were firing on him and after, after Ahmici after such a serious, after such a catastrophic crime had been committed, well to kill or to execute five individuals is one thing. And to set people on fire is another thing. To burn them to ashes is another thing. This is the highest form of genocide, when you set people on fire, when you destroy everything. After Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. such an event the 3rd Corps commander took no action. He could not engage in a conflict with the HVO. But when things came to a head in the summer of 1993, when the HVO declared its intentions openly and we could see what they wanted and they wanted to occupy Bosnia and divide Bosnia together with the Republika Srpska army, well, this was the last straw, the last drop. So then the 3rd Corps tried to deal with the situation and save the corps, prevent the corps from completely falling apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let me turn to a different topic. Earlier this morning, and again this is page 22, lines 20 through 23, in response to a question from the Presiding Judge, you told us about President Izetbegovic visiting some of the positions held by units of the 1st Corps. And my question to you, sir, is: Were you aware of any visits by President Izetbegovic to the 3rd Corps area to include any of its subordinate units during the period late 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I know that in 1993 and later he visited the 1st Corps, my corps. President Izetbegovic left Sarajevo and returned to Sarajevo very frequently without my knowledge. I'm not sure whether this should be said or not, but it's not a secret, he did it with Fikret Prevljak, the commander of the division who I replaced, probably because the president did not completely trust me, President Izetbegovic. I know that later on, in 1994 and 1995, he visited all corps with the exception of the 5th Corps. This was never concealed. This was always information relayed by the television, by the radio. There was also information provided on visits of the president of the state in order to raise combat morale. There were such visits. I can't really tell you when and where, but there were such visits. But in 1994 and 1995, they were particularly frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, General, I asked that because you've referred in your report to having access to the Prosecution exhibits, and one of those exhibits is actually a video segment which has been burned on to a CD. Did you look at any of those videotape segments on any of the material that you were provided by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw some videos of conversations in which leaders of foreigners were involved but I'm not quite sure what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I will move on, sir. You mentioned -- this is the final area I believe that I had a couple of questions about. You mentioned earlier on a couple of occasions forward command posts. And you also, in passing, mentioned, I believe, a Supreme Command Staff forward command post in Kakanj, and I'm wondering if you can tell us when that forward command post was established to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that throughout 1992 and up until the summer of 1993 there was a forward command post of the Supreme Command Staff in Visoko. And then after the tunnel had been made on the first of August, 1993 I believe that after that date in the second half of 1993 or at the end of 1993, this forward command post in Visoko was transferred to Kakanj and certain number of officers from the Supreme Command Staff in Sarajevo went there via the tunnel. But it was established in Kakanj in the second half of 1993 or later on, but I can't tell you when exactly. I don't know the exact month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. General, I would like to come back on some of the questions which were posed to you by the Presiding Judge in these proceedings. And the first issue I would like to cover is the activities of a corps commander or the normal or typical day of a corps commander. My first question relates to the peacetime situation, when you mentioned that the commander of the corps, when he arrives at work, after receiving an oral report and then a written report which was waiting for him on his desk, he would gather his assistants. I would just like to confirm with you whether these assistants are his commanders or whether they are his principal staff officers, meaning G1, G2, G3, G4, and G5. Who are these assistants?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter. Assistants and commanders is two separate things. Commanders of units are commanders of units. A commander of a brigade can be far removed from the location of the corps command. So when I was mentioning that meeting that the corps commander had in the morning his assistants come from his command assistant for legal issues, the assistant for morale, the Chief of Staff, the assistant from mobilisation and other assistants. The assistant for logistics, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in your report, General, you have annexes 97, 98, 99, 100, and 101, where you describe the role or the activities which are played by the G1, G2, G3, G4, and G5. My first question to you is, this -- the use of these acronyms from G1 to G 5, when did this begin and was this in use in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't in use in 1993 and we started using this in accordance with NATO standards only after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the use of these acronyms from G1 to G5, is that standard use, for example, in NATO, because you mentioned that you were trying to get the best from the NATO military.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you said that by 10.00 the commander would likely be contacted by his commanders this time. And his commanders, you mentioned brigade commanders, division commanders or Operational Group commanders. I would just like to confirm so that the Trial Chamber is very clear, what was the organisation initially when the 3rd Corps was created, what was the structure, the unit structure. There was a change with the creation of the Operational Groups. And in your report you mention that later Operational Groups were replaced by divisions. Can you just say from year to year what exactly was the structure in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina so that the Trial Chamber is clear on this.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 and perhaps in part of 1993, all of the corps were organised in terms of brigades, that means that they were composed of brigades and of other smaller independent units in contact with the corps command. The corps commander had direct contact with brigade commanders. They had direct contact with the corps commander. In the course of 1993 and in part of 1994, operative groups were formed as temporary groups, and that means that in each operative group there were a number of brigades, three, four, five or six brigades. And each corps had roughly speaking two, three, or four operative groups. Within that system of organisation, the commanders of OGs had direct contact with the corps commander, or rather the corps commander in this system of organisation had direct contact with the commanders of OGs. And not with brigade commanders, because they were at a level which was further down. In 1994 and 1995, OGs were transformed and they became permanent groups called divisions. Nothing in particular was changed within the context I have been describing, the relationship between the division commander and the corps commander remained the same. The corps commander still had direct contact with the division commanders and that system remained in place up until the end of the war, with the exception of the 5th Corps. That was a small corps so it was organised in a somewhat different manner. But in all the other corps, this is how the system was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now just to make clear while you're here, because I want to make sure that the Trial Chamber understands the difference between an Operational Group and a tactical group. Can you explain the difference between the two for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about OGs and tactical groups, was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question relates to, you gave a briefing to the Trial Chamber and you mentioned at one point that a tactical group had been formed within the 3rd Corps to launch combat activities in a specific area in the Ovnak region. The tactical group that was formed then, where does that stand in the structure so that we are -- we provide the maximum information to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: A tactical group, are we excluding formations such as brigades and OGs and divisions and corps. This is a structure within the vertical organisation of the entire ABiH. A tactical group is similar to these other bodies in terms of organisation, but a tactical group is formed for a particular task, in order to carry out a particular task. Once the task has been carried out all the units that are formed as a tactical group return to their original units. A tactical group can be formed by a commander of an OG or a commander of a division, and it can also be formed by a corps commander or the Main Staff commander. It depends on who forms the tactical group, at which level tactical group. But depending on who forms it you have various levels of units that form the tactical group. The size of the tactical group can vary. A tactical group is established by order of a command, or groups of battalions can be part of a tactical group, or brigades. A commander of a tactical group is appointed. He is given a certain number of men from various units, Able-bodied men and capable officers. A command post is formed. The commanders of the units in the tactical group report to the commander of the tactical group. They are given tasks, or a task, a combat task, carry out the task, and once the task has been carried out the tactical group is disbanded and a report is then sent to the person who established the tactical group, or a report is sent to him on the task that has been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I now move on to the wartime scenario, in terms of a typical day of a commander. And you mentioned that the major difference was that a commander of a corps in wartime does not know what he will be doing the next day. And you also said that -- and you gave a lot of information concerning where you slept during the four years that you were a corps commander. What I would like to know from you is, how many hours a night does a corps commander sleep in wartime, and when you say that the commander does not know what he will be doing the next day, can we reduce down to the commander does not know what he will be doing the next two hours or so?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the degree of combat activities. Very often a corps commander would find himself in the situation in which he wouldn't know what he would be doing in the -- within the next couple of hours. That was a very common situation. And when I look what I did - and again I will go back to the issue of sleeping - I spent a lot of time sleeping in various vehicles, in the jeep which was our command vehicle. I was constantly on the move from one unit to another. I would sleep in the vehicle, or if I was on the way to the central part of Bosnia, I would sleep in the helicopter from Zenica to Tarcin, this area was accessible to the helicopter. So I slept wherever I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, in respect of the time schedule of the corps commander in wartime I would like you to -- you say that, or you said that the corps commander would have to meet with civilians who would come to his office or who would complain to politicians even though that you-- the corps commander was not responsible for the problems they brought to him. Now, on the issue of civilians, did it happen to you or did you meet with internationals or representatives of the international community, and did that take a lot of your time as the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to give you an example. In one part of your question, you mentioned the context of relationship between civilians and the corps commander. For example, in June and August -- July and August, 1993, when I was to be appointed the commander of the 1st Corps, I was amidst combat activities on the mountain of Igman near Sarajevo, and I didn't know that I would be appointed a corps commander. I heard it on the radio and I was surprised, I was taken by surprise. Before that, I saw a list that my predecessor had, my predecessor who wanted to be removed from the position of the corps commander. The list contained the names of 20 people and it was drafted by somebody from the Main Staff, or politicians and I was in the 20th place, the last place. And the 19 preceding names were civilians, politicians. Presidents of municipalities, ministers and so on and so forth. Later on I found out that none of the 19 civilians on the list wanted to take the responsibility of being the commander of the 1st Corps. And then an issue was -- an order was issued saying: Karavelic, it is you. And that is the truth. Later on a number of these people who were involved in politics and who were sitting in their offices or in the cellars, did the things that I mentioned as an example. For example, presidents of municipalities would give money to their respective brigades, bypassing me. I had meetings with civilians. They wanted to meet with me. I would call such meetings and those meetings were worthless. There were no results out of these meetings. And I also had a number, a huge number of meetings with international bodies and individuals representing international organisations in Sarajevo in 1994 and 1995 I met with a number of ambassadors who had arrived in Sarajevo. They came to my office with -- to meet me. I had a number of meetings with attaches of foreign embassies and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. With respect to the activities of the corps commander of course this would include the activities of the command of the corps, and the expert for the Prosecution, General Reinhardt said that, from his reading of the evidence, there were some down time in the activities of the 3rd Corps where the corps could catch up and basically had more time to look at routine matters going on in 1993. Now, I would like to know, from you, from your reading of the documents and the material that was given to you, whether you would agree with General Reinhardt that there were such downtime or times where we could catch up with routine activities in the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand your question well, I can say that from time to time in other corps there were such intervals of low activity or no combat activity. In my corps, in the 1st Corps, this happened very rarely, so rarely that it's even not to be mentioned because there was constant fighting around Sarajevo and in Sarajevo for years. And even if there were such periods of low activity, every corps commander prayed to God for such periods to happen so that he could catch up with things that he couldn't do during the times of combat. And this was to do with the manoeuvre and deployment of units, the logistics of his units and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my question in this respect, General, is, I would like to get your opinion, as an expert, based on the material that you have seen, and was the situation -- what was the situation like in the 3rd Corps command, if you can tell from the documents that you've seen. Were there such downtime or some times where they could catch up?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to say that. In order for my answer to be very precise, I would have to read all the reports of the corps command sent from the operation centre on every day during these four years. I have not read these reports. These reports cover the 24-hour periods indicating the things that happened during those 24-hour periods. I believe that there must have been such lower activity periods. There must have been. But even when there were such periods, such short periods, the corps commander and all the other commanders at lower levels tried to use that time in order to deal with other numerous issues that were directly related with the mission that either the corps of that particular unit had. This had to do with providing for logistics, improving communications in the corps, conversations and contacts with the civilian bodies and institutions, meetings and briefings with their subordinates in the command and in subordinate command; training, replenishment, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reinforcement, ammunition, weapons, and so on and so forth. Let me just give you an example. In 1993, I issued an order according to which a group was established that was to go around Sarajevo and put down all the traffic signs and iron gate around the sport centre called Skenderija. I wanted to use the iron bars to cover them and have hand grenades made out of them. I had to do that as the corps commander there were similar such situations elsewhere, depending on the area. The others had to do the same things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just before the break I have a few questions after the break for you, but just I would like to clarify one thing, because when you said something about not reading the -- that you had not read these reports. Now, I'm a bit surprised, because a lot of those reports were given to you. Which ones did you not read? Or can you clarify this part. Maybe I did not get it right in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not read all the reports issued by the operation centre of the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You did not read -- you read those that you have, but there's some that you did not have? I don't understand. I would like you to clarify whether there are some that you did not have, or is it that you did not read some of the material that you have?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely what you say. When you asked me how many periods of low activity there were in the 3rd Corps, I told you that I would have to consult the reports issued from the 1st of January to the 31st of December, 1993. And then I would be able to come up with the periods of time when there was no combat engaging the 3rd Corps units. This is what I said and this is why I told you that I cannot answer your question, because it would be only these 24-hour reports that would give me an insight into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that it is the time for another break. And after the break I believe that I will need only 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the break we will have only 45 minutes and you're saying that you need 30 minutes and I hope that Mr. Dixon will not need more than 15 minutes in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I will need only two minutes. There is only one matter that we wish to clarify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We shall resume at five to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you have 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have spoken with my client and with the General, and I will try to be as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, this is the last stretch. My next question simply has to do with what you mentioned concerning the possibility for a corps commander where he may have to "go on the spot," to use your own words. And you mentioned that you yourself actually went very close to the front lines and that you actually spoke to soldiers. Now in this respect, I would like to know what, if you can make a difference between the situation of the 1st Corps in this respect and the possibility for the commander of the 3rd Corps to go to the front lines and, I would like you to address, in this respect, the difference in size of the corps area and, even more importantly, the difference in freedom of movement, whereas whether it was possible for the 3rd commander to travel to the front line and also if you can add rest the issue of the risk, whereby, is it better for a corps commander to go himself or to send representatives due to the risk of the commander being captured. Can you speak about this issue?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle commanders and particularly commanders of operations, formations such as a corps, should spend most of the time in their main command posts. I don't rule out a possibility of the corps commander visiting his immediately subordinate units for a number of reasons. However, in normal circumstances, it is very rare for a corps commander to go to visit a brigade, battalion, a company, or a platoon. They simply don't do that. In the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the circumstances were different and I myself had to do it in a number of situations. I simply had to do it, to avoid disastrous consequences. And I did it of my own accord. Nobody asked me to do that. I simply knew I had to do it. Very often I would send somebody to represent me, but very often people on the ground asked to see the commander and nobody else but the commander. And in such cases no representative could do what I could do. At the same time, it was not popular and it was not militarily feasible for the commander -- for the corps commander to ramble around as he wanted. And it was not good for them to be exposed to danger, to the danger of being killed or to become a target of the fifth column or somebody else, of being captured or stopped at checkpoints by somebody. All this would have put the corps commander in the situation of being removed from his ranks and from the corps, being left without a leader. This is a very dangerous situation in the times of war, and that is why the rules of service do not foresee such a situation, for a situation in which the corps commander would be exposed to risks and danger. However in Bosnia-Herzegovina, things were ought of the ordinary and that's why I did the things that I did. I believe that the other commanders did the same to a greater or lesser extent. Maybe I would have done it even to a bigger extent, but every time did I it, I had a problem leaving Sarajevo. I had to do it during the night. When I used the tunnel under the airport in Sarajevo, I would reach a slope at the foot of Igman, and this area was constantly shelled by the enemy and nobody could cross it during the day. The 3rd Corps commander had HVO checkpoints especially when they became engaged in fighting against the HVO and all of these checkpoints posed a danger for the corps commander to be captured or to be kidnapped, like Totic was in Zenica. And this would not have been good for the 3rd Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Specifically related question: When you said that, in response to a question by the Presiding Judge, that it was not possible for the corps commanders to meet before August of 1993 and you said specifically that the commander of 5 Corps could never be there. In very short terms, why could the commander of 5 Corps, why could he not be there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in territorial terms, physically he was completely separated from the territories of the other four corps. The 5th Corps was in control of Bihac and its surroundings, the four or five municipalities, the 6th was taken by Fikret Abdic and the only way he could access the area was by means of the international forces' helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That meeting that you mentioned of the corps commanders in August of 1993 was convened at the initiative of General Hadzihasanovic and that the creation of the seventh corps is something that was discussed on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which meeting are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The meeting of the corps commanders, the one you referred to when you responded to the question of the Presiding Judge, which took place in August of 1993. Do you remember who -- at whose initiative was this meeting convened and whether that the issue was of the creation of the 7th corps was discussed on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was the only meeting in Zenica in August and it was also the first meeting at which corps commanders, without the 5th Corps commander, reported to the commander of the Main Staff about all the elements of combat readiness for their respective corps and the objective was to look at the current political and military situation. And to decide on the elements and goals in the forthcoming period and I suppose that this meeting was called at the initiative of the commander of the Main Staff. I believe that that was the case and this meeting was held in Zenica, in one of the buildings in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I move on to the issue of communications, which was raised by the Presiding Judge. And the question related to the way in which the Supreme Command Staff or the Main Staff could contact the corps commands. And you did give -- you provided a reply as to how it was done. Now, my question to you is: You've seen a lot of the communication or the reports which were exchanged between the Supreme Command and the corps. But we have a witness who appeared before this Trial Chamber, a communications specialist, and that is Zivko Sakib and he mentioned that in respect of the Paket communications, which you referred to, that it was regularly necessary to try up to ten times before we could succeed in getting one message across. Is that a situation that you are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less so. Due to the poor quality of communication links I was talking about the repeaters where they were placed, at what angles, what was the radio access range to these repeaters, what their par was, what was the reception of radio signals, and so on and so forth. These were all problems, huge problems and if you add to that the influence of the enemy in interfering with these communication lines, this compounded the situation even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this is a very important question, General. We have in the material which was given to you a number of pieces of paper or communications which were exchanged between the 3rd Corps and the Supreme Command. Now I'm asking you as both an expert and someone who was -- lived through this situation, what should we conclude by the number of communications between 3rd Corps and the Supreme Command? Does that mean that there were communications as much as they would have liked? Or actually what you saw is only the tip of the iceberg, in terms of what should have taken place between the Supreme Command and the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would sooner say that it was a very low hill, when it comes to the communications between the 3rd Corps and the command. My situation was much more favourable. When I was in Sarajevo, I could go to the commander of the Main Staff or even to the members of the Supreme Command in order to seek a device or talk to them. What I'm saying here is that, a direct contact between two commanders, a superior and a subordinate, is the best way of communication, and the safest way of communication. Although a contact may be through a physical presence or by telephone, the 3rd Corps commander did not have the opportunity to have either of the two. The 3rd Corps commander did not have the opportunity to talk to the Main Staff. On the 21st or 22nd of August, when there was a meeting in Zenica, he was -- his first contact from the time when he left Sarajevo. Even when he spoke to the Main Staff on the telephone, he could not talk about any serious security issues, because all the telephone lines were intercepted. There was no way for anybody to use telephone to talk about any serious military issues or combat operations, and the only means that he had was Paket communication. And we know that a thought can never be conveyed in writing as it can be in a direct personal contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The Presiding Judge put a question to you with respect to paragraphs 283 and 287 of your report, in terms of how political control was exercised. I would just like you to confirm, based on your report, that there is a difference between the principle of subordination of the army to the state, and the exercise of command and control over military units, that this is two different things. Based on your report, do you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will say again. The principle of subordination of the army to the state, based on your report would mean that the army does not decide, the army does what the state wants it to do. And also in your report you discuss what is effective control and what is the exercise of command and control over a command, over military units. Is this two different things?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure I have fully understood your question. While the Supreme Command Staff existed, the very term "Supreme Command Staff" points to the fact that it was the staff that had operative and staff functions to perform on behalf of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Later it was transformed, the Supreme Command Staff was transformed into the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to provide it with more responsibility when it came to command and control. When it came to the command and control of military units of the ABiH and, to be more precise, the Supreme Command, as the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina is the supreme military authority. It is responsible for issuing orders, political orders, issuing political directives, and by issuing political directives from the Supreme Command the Main Staff of the ABiH takes action. And then this is forwarded lower down the chain between the Supreme Command of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Main Staff. We also have the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Ministry of Defence attached to these bodies, and they have their own responsibilities and powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. An issue which was raised by the Presiding Judge is that of civilian casualties or collateral damage, following combat activities. I would like to know from you, as an expert, when there are combat activities, whether there are people whose responsibility it is to gather this information, and that whether this is something that would -- that the corps commander would be looking for before he gets the reports from those who are responsible from collecting this information.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the corps command and the corps as a whole, there are no specific individuals who have the duty of looking into collateral damage. And at the same time with regard to the second part of your question, collateral damage is not a particular issue, in that it would be a subject of -- corps command would focus on and ask for reports about such damage. If collateral damage, serious collateral damage has been observed, the commanders of the units in the field have to report --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge put a question to you looking for foreigners who came to Bosnia, and I will say in French the exact words, [Interpretation] "to provide assistance to the ABiH." [In English] Now, you said that in the 1st Corps you did have a German who came, who became a member of the 1st Corps, stayed for a year and then he left. But then you said -- no, no. You said he was killed. Sorry. Then you said that there were no larger group of this kind, and you said the only exception was 3rd Corps ^^^. So my first question is, did you know that there were foreigners in Tesanj in the 3rd Corps, in Bacilja [phoen], and also in the 2nd [sic], in Guzin [phoen] in the 5th Corps, and in other areas in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that you have mentioned the fact, I do remember it. But what you said about the 2nd Corps is something that I thought concerned the 3rd Corps in the Central Bosnian area, although that is in an area that divides the territory of the first and 2nd Corps. But I heard about something of that kind in relation to the 5th Corps, but I don't have reliable information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now when you said there was an exception for the 3rd Corps and I compare with your report, did you mean that these groups were cooperating with the army? Or as you said in your report, that they were not cooperating with the army? I'd just like to clarify what you said when you responded, the only exception was in the area of the 3rd Corps. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that the 3rd Corps was covering most of the territory of Central Bosnia, if not all of the territory. At the same time that territory was a more suitable area in which one could obtain information Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. on these foreign volunteers. And they were mostly concentrated in that central part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is where their main sanctuary was located, and that is what guided me in terms of the question that you've just put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You're saying there were some groups of foreign volunteers on the territory of the 3rd Corps, but not in the units of the 3rd Corps because the presiding -- the questions from the Presiding Judge was "in the strength of units of the 3rd Corps"?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mean that they were in 3rd Corps units and that is not something that I am claiming now. They were not part of the 3rd Corps units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question, General, deals with the issue of weapons. And specifically with the question of tanks. Now, of course, if we want to use a tank, we need fuel and we need ammunition. For example, we have a witness called Ribo Haso who said that in any one time he could no longer -- he could not have more fuel or he could not have fuel to run a vehicle for more than one hour. Did you have the ammunition and the fuel to run the tanks that you had in the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me a minute or two. In spite of the fact that we're running out of time, in the last four to five years, I had very serious problems with investigators from The Hague Tribunal, because they would come to Sarajevo and they would try at any cost to find -- well, let's say, ten or a hundred tanks, because let's say they would receive information from the Serbian side. On the basis of those reports that were drafted at the time in the course of the war they would go to Sarajevo. Several hundred times when these investigators came to Sarajevo I had to show them various places in Sarajevo. And I had to explain to them that there weren't more than five tanks in Sarajevo. They couldn't understand that. They probably heard other information from the other side. And that is understandable, but out of those five tanks could not be used because we had no spare parts and three tanks that we had were always kept as firing positions, that's how we put it in military terms. It would be dug in, to a -- at a certain position because we had no fuel for the tanks. If I wanted to move the tank, then I would move the tank from one position to another position. That would be once a month or perhaps every two months, provided that I had obtained a sufficient amount of fuel to do this. In addition, throughout the war in Sarajevo, and in particular in 1993, I as the corps commander drove around in a golf. I spent a lot of time driving around in a golf, not to say -- in a golf car, not to say the entire year. And this vehicle used oil from transformation stations, from all transformation stations. In all of those transformation stations, they have 20, 30 or 100 litres of oil in -- there are a lot of such transformation stations in Sarajevo and this is the fuel we would take from those stations and this is the fuel that we would use for the golfs, which turned out to be extremely appropriate and a significant contribution made by civilisation to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If you go to 513 and 514, you say that the army was extremely poorly armed and that there was an average of one weapon for three soldiers, and that regarding ammunition, the most difficult period was in 1993. Do you agree with what you said in your report? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. That was the case in my corps and the situation was no better in the other corps. On average we had one rifle for three men or one rifle for even more men and as far as ammunition and other equipment is concerned, 1993 was the most difficult year because nothing arrived from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina because the HVO had sealed off all the borders and had established control over all the roads. That is the problem that the 3rd Corps commander and the 3rd Corps and the entire army in summer of 1993, to reach the point at the top of the pyramid that I described a while ago. And local production was simply not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like you to turn to your report at paragraphs 638 which is an issue that was raised by the Presiding Judge, where you said that if - I will wait until you have paragraph 638 --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: 138? I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 638. Now, in this paragraph, you say that "if unknown individuals" - and later you say that this includes foreign fighters, or groups of individuals - "are present in the area of responsibility without being under his command and control, a corps commander is not responsible for their actions." Now, you said this and other witnesses have confirmed this. What I would like you to comment on is paragraph 642 where it says that: "All of the above shows that the presence of individuals or groups of individuals who were not under the command and control of the corps, is not an issue which should distract a corps commander from the accomplishment of his mission." And then you go on to say: "On the contrary, in accordance with the accepted principles of armed combat, what is expected from a corps commander in such circumstances is that no more than the absolute necessary attention, time and resources to ensure that the presence of such elements will not impede the accomplishment of the mission of the Corps will be devoted to this issue." Can you elaborate on this paragraph specifically, in as few words as possible.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, the last sentence in this paragraph, 642, is the key sentence which clarifies everything. A corps commander cannot and does not have to focus on something that has no direct bearing on the accomplishment of his mission. If a problem arises such as the problem with the foreigners, as this problem becomes increasingly serious, and as the way they affect the way in which the corps mission will be accomplished, as this happens the corps commander starts focussing on this problem, or starts to focus increasingly on this problem. So it depends on the extent to which they pose a threat to the mission of the corps. If the threat becomes increasingly serious, the corps commander has to start paying more and more attention to this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My next question is again a problem raised by the Presiding Judge and also by my colleague, and that is: Did the 3rd Corps successfully accomplish its mission or did it barely survive and avoid catastrophe in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want a very brief answer, then I would say that it barely survived and managed to avoid an even more serious catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my last question is: In ensuring that a catastrophe was avoided, did General Hadzihasanovic, in your expert opinion, exercise his command in a responsible manner and did he neglect any of his duties as a corps commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowing General Enver Hadzihasanovic, I couldn't even imagine that he acted in an irresponsible way or that he failed to act in a serious manner. And similarly I can't imagine that General Hadzihasanovic, given his character, would allow himself to act in violation of the rules and regulations, in spite of the fact that -- or regardless of the fact that there were tasks he had to carry out and he had to respect all the rules and regulations when carrying them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much General. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This concludes my re-examination that arises from the Judge's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: General, just one question. You mentioned that the forward command post of the Supreme Command was moved to Kakanj town. Do you know the location within the town that it was moved to?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forward command post was moved to three buildings. There was a DC building that had some office space and that is where equipment and supplies were kept for the town of Kakanj, and across the road from that building there was a petrol station which is where, in the course of 1993 and 1994, we had frequent meetings and subsequently the Sretno Motel was also used. I don't know the exact dates, though. So that is a compound, in a circle of about 200 or 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Just for the transcript the motel that you mentioned, could you just spell that out as it hasn't been recorded properly in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sretno motel. The S-r-e-t-n-o motel. Sretno.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, General. This brings your testimony to the end. You have spent two weeks in The Hague and you have answered the questions put to you by Defence counsel, the Prosecution and by myself. I would like to thank you for your contribution to establishing the truth. And on behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish you all the best when returning to your country and I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we adjourn, there are two issues I would like to raise. There is a problem that concerns the 92 bis procedure I believe, the procedure has not yet been carried out and there are certain translations problems. According to what I have been told, you won't have the statements before next Friday. Next Friday is when you will provide us with your motion. As a result, there is the question of the Prosecution's position, but I believe that there are no difficulties that we have encountered and before we start hearing General Kubura's witnesses, the Chamber has to render a decision with regard to tendering into evidence these 92 bis statements. If the Prosecution does not object. But the Prosecution will inform us of their position. But if there are no objections, just before we hear the first witness for Mr. Kubura, we could render an oral decision because obviously we won't have the time to render a written decision. Mr. Mundis, what is the Prosecution's position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We've been provided with copies of a number of proposed 92 bis witness statements. We have indicated to the Defence that we have no objection to those 92 bis statements being admitted into evidence, nor do we seek the leave of the Trial Chamber to have those witnesses appear for purposes of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Defence counsel is then in a position to confirm that by next Friday we should have everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite right, Mr. President. Could we go into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now that we are in open session, we should be resuming our work, not next Monday but the Monday after that. Mr. Dixon, could you confirm that all the witnesses will be available by that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have already given our list of witnesses to Your Honours and the Prosecution for the first week. They will all be arriving next week, so they will be available to testify. I should just clarify, Your Honour that we will use our opportunity to make an opening speech on Monday, the 11th of April. After the 92 bis matter has been finalised. It won't be a lengthy opening, but it will take up some time and we expect the first witness to at least start on Monday, but probably then continue on Tuesday. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As I have another hearing at 2.15, are there any other issues you would like to raise? But it is necessary to adjourn very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. Very briefly, Mr. President, we forgot to tender this document into evidence. I don't know if my colleague objects. It's the table and forms of subordination that is based on the witness's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, could we have a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is Defence Exhibit DH2089, and we have an English version, I believe. It's just one document, very well. DH2089. Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If there are no other issues to be dealt with, I invite you all to return at the hearing that will commence not next Monday but the Monday after that at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of April, 2005, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
